questions.question: An onClick handler writes to two different State objects, both read by the same composable. How is that composable recomposed?
options: Twice, synchronously, once inside each assignment
Once, synchronously, at the end of the click handler
Twice, on two consecutive frames
Once, in a single pass on the next frame
questions.explanation: State writes only mark the reading scopes invalid; the Recomposer then waits for the next frame and recomposes all invalid scopes together. Assignments never run composition inline, so multiple writes in one event are batched into one pass.

questions.question: When a state value changes, Compose invalidates only the restartable scopes that read it, rather than recomposing the whole tree from the root.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reads are recorded per recompose scope, so a change invalidates just those scopes, and children with unchanged inputs may be skipped. This is why where you read state matters: reading it higher up widens how much is recomposed.

questions.question: Which scope is invalidated when `count` changes?
options: The Screen function, because `count` is declared there
The Button's content lambda, where `count` is read
Only Title, since it is the first child of the Column
The whole Activity content that was set by setContent
questions.explanation: With a `by` delegate the State is read where `count` is used, which is inside Button's content lambda. Composable lambdas get their own restart scope, so only that lambda re-runs. Declaring state somewhere does not subscribe that scope; reading it does.

questions.question: Why does reading state directly inside a Column { } block recompose the composable that contains the Column?
options: Column is an inline function, so its content has no restart scope of its own
Column is marked @NonSkippable, which forces its parent to recompose
Column copies every child's state reads up to the root composition
Column caches its children, so it must invalidate the parent to refresh them
questions.explanation: Column, Row and Box are inline, so their content lambda is inlined into the caller and reads there belong to the caller's scope. Extracting the reading code into its own composable gives it a separate scope and narrows recomposition.

questions.question: Which statements about MonotonicFrameClock are true? Select all that apply.
options: withFrameNanos suspends until the next frame and passes that frame's time
On Android the clock used by Compose UI is driven by Choreographer
withFrameNanos returns immediately with System.nanoTime() of the call
Compose animations read frame times from the clock in their coroutine context
The Recomposer runs a separate pass for each state write, without a clock
questions.explanation: The Recomposer and animations wait on the frame clock found in the coroutine context; on Android it is backed by Choreographer vsync. This is also why tests can control time through the test clock. Recomposition is frame-aligned and batched, not per write.

questions.question: A coroutine on Dispatchers.Default sets `state.value = x` without any explicit snapshot. What happens?
options: It crashes with CalledFromWrongThreadException, as Views would
The write is lost unless it is wrapped in withContext(Dispatchers.Main)
It writes the global snapshot; a later apply notice invalidates readers
It immediately recomposes the readers on that background thread
questions.explanation: Snapshot state is thread-safe: a write outside an explicit snapshot goes to the global snapshot. Compose arranges for global changes to be sent as apply notifications, the Recomposer maps the changed objects to the scopes that read them and schedules a frame. Recomposition then runs on the Recomposer's own thread, not the writer's.

questions.question: Writing to a state object during composition, after that same state has already been read in the current composition, can cause an endless recomposition loop.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: This is a 'backwards write': the write invalidates a scope that has just read the old value, so it must run again, writes again, and so on, every frame. State should be written in event handlers or effects, not in the composable body.

questions.question: A header follows scroll position. Why is `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, -scroll.value) }` cheaper than `Modifier.offset(y = (-scroll.value).dp)`?
options: The lambda version runs on a background thread instead of the main thread
The lambda reads state in layout, so scrolling skips recomposition
The lambda version is cached, so it only runs on the first frame
The dp version allocates a Dp object, which triggers garbage collection
questions.explanation: In the value version, scroll.value is read during composition, so every pixel of scroll recomposes the caller. In the lambda version the read happens inside the layout phase, so only the layout scope is invalidated and composition is skipped. Both run on the main thread every frame.

questions.question: Which of these can make a restartable composable scope recompose? Select all that apply.
options: A State it read in its last composition changes
Its parent recomposes and passes a changed parameter
A state it never read is written to
A compositionLocalOf value it reads changes
invalidate() is called on the host ComposeView
questions.explanation: A scope reruns when something it read changes (state or a dynamic CompositionLocal) or when its caller reruns and its inputs differ. Writes to state it never read don't touch it. View.invalidate() only asks for a redraw of the View; it doesn't invalidate composition scopes.

questions.question: Why wrap `listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0` in `remember { derivedStateOf { ... } }` when deciding whether to show a scroll-to-top button?
options: So readers recompose only when the Boolean result flips
So the value is saved across process death with the scroll position
So the comparison runs on a background thread off the main thread
Because firstVisibleItemIndex cannot be read in composition otherwise
questions.explanation: Read directly, every change of the index invalidates the reader even though the Boolean stays the same. derivedStateOf only notifies its readers when its computed result changes. It doesn't save state or move work off the main thread.
